profiles.meeting_scenario: At a university-affiliated training and research hospital, the pediatric surgery service is trying to sustain and standardize SBAR use after an initial implementation effort showed improved questionnaire scores but mixed nurse perceptions about time burden. This coordination meeting is between the pediatric surgery charge nurse, who oversees daily handover practice across two inpatient units, and the nursing education/quality coordinator, who is preparing the next hospital quality committee update and the ongoing monitoring plan. The agenda is to align on current rollout status, what counts in the uptake numbers, which SBAR materials are being used on the units, and what evidence will be presented as the next milestone. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on the reporting workflow and readiness for the next review checkpoint.

members.name: Elif Demir
members.expertise: Shift handover operations, inpatient pediatric surgical care, charge nurse workflow coordination
members.background: Elif has worked for six years on pediatric surgery wards and now coordinates staffing and bedside handovers across two neighboring units; she was one of the local champions who helped introduce SBAR to the nursing team.
members.private_state: She wants the rollout to be seen as workable by bedside nurses and is especially concerned that extra documentation demands will revive complaints that SBAR wastes time during busy shifts.
hidden_assumptions: A 'completed SBAR' means the nurse used the SBAR structure in verbal handover and had the form present, even if some fields were left brief or blank.
When people discuss 'handover' on pediatric surgery, they usually mean routine shift-to-shift exchange on the inpatient ward, not return reports from PACU or OR.
The unit can slightly adapt the SBAR paper form for local needs as long as the four SBAR headings remain visible.
A unit is 'ready' for the next quality review once nurses are consistently using SBAR without incidents, major resistance, or obvious workflow disruption.

members.name: Dr. Kerem Aydin
members.role: Nursing Education and Quality Improvement Coordinator
members.expertise: Clinical training rollout, audit design, nursing documentation quality, hospital quality reporting
members.background: Kerem is a nurse educator with a doctorate in health services quality and manages hospital-wide training materials, audit tools, and committee reporting for communication-safety initiatives.
members.private_state: He wants the pediatric surgery units to produce documentation that can be compared cleanly across units and fed into the hospital dashboard without having to rework the data.
hidden_assumptions: A 'completed SBAR' means all four sections are documented clearly enough to be scored against the handover rating checklist.
For pediatric surgery reporting, 'handover' should include any nurse-to-nurse transfer where communication risk is material, including returns from PACU or OR.
The 'SBAR form' refers to the official standardized version stored by the education office, because version consistency is necessary for audit comparability.
A unit is 'ready' for the next quality committee update only when there is auditable evidence of sustained use across both units, not just smooth day-to-day operation.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a completed SBAR
misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss 'completion' or 'completed SBARs' as if it were a single obvious metric.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elif means that the SBAR structure was used in the verbal handover and the form was used or present, even if some sections were sparsely filled.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Kerem means that each of the four SBAR sections is documented sufficiently to be scored as a full SBAR record.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In routine implementation talk, 'completion' sounds like standard administrative language, so both assume the institution already has a shared definition and neither feels a need to unpack it.

misalignment_points.topic: Which handovers are included in the numbers
misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to 'handover uptake' or 'handover numbers' for the pediatric surgery units.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elif is counting routine ward shift-change handovers between outgoing and incoming nurses on the inpatient units.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Kerem is counting those handovers plus clinically important nurse-to-nurse transfers tied to pediatric surgery patients, such as PACU-to-ward returns.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are speaking about the same patients and the same service line, so the difference in boundary feels too operationally obvious to mention unless someone explicitly audits the denominator.

misalignment_points.topic: Which SBAR form is the current one
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both mention 'the SBAR form' as though there is only one active artifact.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elif is thinking of the locally reprinted bedside paper sheet currently used by her units, which keeps SBAR headings but adds lines for drains and parent concerns.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Kerem is thinking of the official education-office template kept on the hospital shared drive and used for formal audit comparison.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both artifacts are recognizably SBAR forms with the same core headings, so surface references feel interchangeable and cooperative rather than discrepant.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to be ready for the quality committee update
misalignment_points.surface_form: They say the units will be 'ready' for the next quality committee review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elif means the staff are using SBAR routinely enough that handovers are smoother, no safety problems have appeared, and frontline resistance has settled down.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Kerem means there is enough standardized, auditable evidence of use to present as a credible implementation status to the committee.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Readiness language in coordination meetings often functions as a reassuring status label, and both assume the other is using the usual institutional benchmark without stating the underlying threshold.

turns.inner_thought: Since the refresher sessions, the bedside nurses on both inpatient pediatric surgery wards have settled back into using SBAR during routine shift-to-shift report. What matters to me is that it no longer feels like an extra burden and nobody is grumbling the way they did early on. If I frame this as stable and workable, Kerem should see that the rollout is holding without pushing for anything that adds more writing.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. From the unit side, things have settled quite a bit since the refresher sessions. Across the two pediatric surgery units, SBAR use has stabilized, and the handovers are feeling more routine again for both day and night teams.

turns.inner_thought: Good start. I need to know whether they're actually ready for next month's quality committee review, meaning I can show sustained, auditable use across both units in a way that fits the dashboard. If the rollout only feels smoother locally but I can't extract comparable evidence, that won't help me.
turns.utterance: That’s encouraging. I mainly want to be sure we’re on track for next month’s quality committee update. From your side, how is the rollout looking operationally, and do you feel the units are getting ready for the next review?

turns.inner_thought: Operationally, yes. For the ward shift handovers I oversee, nearly everyone is using SBAR verbally and keeping the form with them, even if some boxes are brief. I’m not thinking about PACU or OR return reports here; when we talk handover uptake on pediatric surgery, I mean the regular ward exchanges on the two units.
turns.utterance: Overall it looks good. We’re seeing almost full completion on SBAR during day and night handovers on both wards, and handover uptake has been steady enough that it’s no longer something charge nurses have to chase every shift.

turns.inner_thought: If their completed SBARs remain high when I pull the post-training handover set, that could be enough for the committee summary—as long as the records are complete enough to score and the sample covers the pediatric surgery handover activity I’m expecting. This sounds promising for readiness, assuming the audit data holds up.
turns.utterance: That’s helpful to hear. If completion stays high once the post-training handover set is pulled, I can work that into the committee summary. It would make the update much easier if the pattern holds and the units are moving toward being ready.

turns.inner_thought: The nurses are comfortable because we’ve been using the bedside paper version adapted for our unit, with the same SBAR headings but extra lines for drains and parent concerns. That local tweak made it practical. I should mention it positively, so he knows staff have accepted the SBAR form without feeling boxed in.
turns.utterance: One thing that’s helped is that the nurses are comfortable with the SBAR form they have at the bedside. That version has been easier for them to work with in real time, especially on the pediatric surgery side.

turns.inner_thought: Good, as long as we're all referring to the official SBAR form from the education office. I need version consistency so the audits are comparable across units and I don’t end up cleaning unusable data. I’ll signal that I’m sticking with the standard template, but I don’t think there’s any real discrepancy here.
turns.utterance: That’s good to know. On my end, I’ll keep using the SBAR form from the education shared drive so the audits stay comparable. If the teams are already comfortable with the form, that should make the monitoring smoother.

turns.inner_thought: I can send the Friday counts the charge nurses collect from the routine ward handovers they directly supervise each shift. Those are the meaningful numbers for how the units are actually functioning. I’m not planning to include PACU-to-ward or OR return reports because those aren’t what we usually mean when we discuss handover numbers on the ward.
turns.utterance: I can send you Friday’s numbers from the charge nurses so you have something current. The handover numbers we’ve been tracking are based on the regular ward handovers they supervise each shift, and those counts have looked quite consistent lately.

turns.inner_thought: That will help, though for the dashboard I’m trying to capture the full pediatric surgery handover picture, not only shift change. Still, her numbers are a useful start, and if I combine them with the post-training material I may be able to show progress toward readiness. She sounds confident, so she probably assumes the data stream is straightforward.
turns.utterance: Yes, send those through. That should help me build the picture for the dashboard, because I’m trying to capture the full pediatric surgery handover uptake as the units move toward readiness. Even an updated interim set will be useful for the next step.

turns.inner_thought: From the frontline perspective, we’ll be ready soon if the next couple of weeks stay calm: nurses keep using SBAR, no new complaints about time burden, no incidents, no disruption. That’s the real threshold for me. Once it’s embedded in routine practice, the committee review should be straightforward.
turns.utterance: From my perspective, we should be ready soon if the next two weeks stay smooth and the team keeps using SBAR the way they are now. As long as there aren’t any fresh complaints and the handovers keep running normally, I’d be comfortable saying the units are ready for the next quality committee review.

turns.inner_thought: I’ll wait for the completed SBARs and the post-implementation material, then draft the committee slide when I have enough auditable evidence to present a solid status update. If the dataset is clean, I can show sustained use across both units without caveats. She seems aligned, so this should be manageable.
turns.utterance: That sounds reasonable. I’ll draft the committee slide once the completed SBARs are in and the post-implementation material is solid enough to present. If that comes together as expected, we should be in a good position for next month’s update.
